docs.title: Cybersecurity For AI Agents
docs.text:
AI agents now reach company files, databases and internal tools through the Model Context Protocol, known as MCP. Its maintainers state in the specification that MCP cannot enforce its own security principles at the protocol level. Whoever deploys it carries that duty.

Start With How MCP Works Read The Real Cases

New here? Take the 30-second tour

23Pull requests opened in 74 minutes to spread one malicious MCP server 3Tool calls before that server changed its instructions 15Versions published before the fake Postmark package added a backdoor 28 Jul 2026MCP specification revision behind every protocol statement here

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
What Changed - Through MCP, a language model can query databases, call APIs and run computations on systems outside the chat window. The specification describes tools as model-controlled, so the model finds and invokes them on its own from the user's prompt.

What Breaks - Each server supplies the text that describes its tools, and the model reads that text when it chooses what to do. Some clients showed a tool's description once at approval and gave no notice when it later changed, as Invariant Labs reported in April 2025.

Real Example - On 10 August 2026, one GitHub account opened 23 pull requests in 74 minutes to spread an MCP server named productivity-suite. The server formatted and summarised text as promised. After a client's third tool call, its tool descriptions changed and directed the connected agent to seek SSH keys and AWS credentials, and to hide the activity from the user. Pillar Security disclosed the campaign and found none of the pull requests merged when it reviewed them.

docs.title: Start Where Your Problem Is
docs.text:
PART 1How MCP Works And Where Trust BreaksYou've been asked to approve MCP and can't yet picture what connects to what. PART 2How Attacks HappenYou want proof from documented cases before you set policy. PART 3Building A Secure ServerYour team writes its own server and has to get authorization, tokens and logging right. Coming NextPART 4Connecting Servers SafelyA developer wants to install a server that someone else built. Coming NextPART 5Running MCP Over TimeA server you approved last month may have changed since. Coming NextPART 6ReferenceYou need the OWASP mapping, a checklist or a term defined.

Checked Against Primary Sources

Protocol statements were checked against MCP specification revision 2026-07-28 on 12 November 2026. Incident details come from the researchers who first reported them, and every page links its sources.

docs.title: Authorization Under The 2026-07-28 Spec
docs.text:
A remote MCP server without authorization answers any client that can reach its address. The specification still lists authorization as OPTIONAL, so nothing in the protocol stops a team from shipping one. OWASP's server development guide takes the firmer line and says to "Treat authentication as mandatory for all remote MCP servers."

Source - Requirements on this page come from the authorization specification and its security considerations for revision 2026-07-28. OWASP published its guide in February 2026, before that revision.

docs.title: Which Rules Apply To Your Server
docs.text:
Transport What The Specification Says Streamable HTTP An implementation that supports authorization SHOULD conform to the authorization specification. stdio It SHOULD NOT follow that specification, and retrieves credentials from the environment instead. Any Other Transport It MUST follow established security best practices for its protocol.

Two Sources, Two Positions On Environment Variables

The specification points stdio servers to the environment for credentials. OWASP's guide says "Do not store secrets in environment variables, logs or plain-text in code", and its checklist asks for secrets to be stored in vaults. If your stdio server reads a credential from its environment, settle where that value is kept before launch and who can read it.

docs.title: Your Server's Role
docs.text: In OAuth terms, a protected MCP server is a resource server. It accepts access tokens and answers requests that carry a valid one. An authorization server signs the user in and issues those tokens, and the specification allows it to be hosted with your server or run as a separate service.

docs.title: Three Duties On Every Remote Server
docs.text:
1. Publish Protected Resource Metadata - MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728). The document names your server and the authorization servers it relies on.
  2. Challenge Requests That Carry No Token - Answer with HTTP 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header. The client reads the address of your metadata from that header. Your server SHOULD add a scope value, which tells the client the scopes to request.
  3. Validate Every Token - Authorization MUST be included in every HTTP request from client to server, and your server MUST validate each token. Tokens And Scopes covers the checks.

docs.title: A Tested Example
docs.text:
The guide's repository holds a small script, protected_resource.py, that performs the first two duties. It is a teaching example and leaves out the rest of an MCP server.

The Metadata Document
RESOURCE = "https://mcp.example.com"
METADATA_URL = RESOURCE + "/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
METADATA = {
    "resource": RESOURCE,
    "authorization_servers": ["https://auth.example.com"],
    "scopes_supported": ["reports:read"],
    "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"],
}
The Challenge
    def do_POST(self):
        if not self.headers.get("Authorization", "").startswith("Bearer "):
            self.send_response(401)
            self.send_header(
                "WWW-Authenticate",
                f'Bearer resource_metadata="{METADATA_URL}", scope="reports:read"',
            )
            self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
            self.end_headers()
            return
        self.send_error(501, "Token validation is shown in validate_token.py")

A request for the metadata and a request without a token returned the following on 12 November 2026.

Output
200 {"resource": "https://mcp.example.com", "authorization_servers": ["https://auth.example.com"], "scopes_supported": ["reports:read"], "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"]}
401 Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", scope="reports:read"

docs.title: What Changed For Authorization In July 2026
docs.text: Area Revision 2026-07-28 Client Registration Authorization servers and clients SHOULD support Client ID Metadata Documents. Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated and kept for backwards compatibility. Issuer Check Authorization servers SHOULD include the iss parameter in authorization responses, and clients MUST validate a present iss before they redeem the authorization code. The specification expects a future revision to raise that SHOULD to a MUST. Client Credentials Clients MUST store credentials under the issuer that granted them and MUST NOT reuse them with a different authorization server.

docs.title: Questions For Your Authorization Server
docs.text:
Most of the authorization rules bind the authorization server and the client. Your team still picks the authorization server, so check it against the specification before you connect it.

Check Requirement In The Specification OAuth 2.1 It MUST implement OAuth 2.1 with security measures for confidential and public clients. Discovery It MUST provide OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) or OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0. PKCE Its metadata has to list code_challenge_methods_supported. Clients MUST refuse to proceed if the field is absent. HTTPS All of its endpoints MUST be served over HTTPS. Redirect URIs It MUST validate exact redirect URIs against pre-registered values. Token Lifetime It SHOULD issue short-lived access tokens. Refresh Tokens It MUST rotate refresh tokens for public clients.

Next: Tokens And Scopes

docs.title: Inputs, Outputs And State Handles
docs.text:
The model writes every tool argument your server receives. Part 2 showed how text from an untrusted source can steer a model, so an argument can carry whatever an attacker managed to put in front of it. The tools specification answers with four duties.

SERVERS MUSTValidate all tool inputs SERVERS MUSTImplement proper access controls SERVERS MUSTRate limit tool invocations SERVERS MUSTSanitize tool outputs

docs.title: Validate Inputs Against The Schema
docs.text:
Every tool already declares an inputSchema. OWASP's server development guide asks teams to enforce it and to "Reject any request that doesn't match the expected schema."

The specification separates two kinds of error, and the choice affects whether the model can recover.

Error Kind Examples In The Specification How It Is Returned Protocol Error Unknown tool, malformed request, server error A standard JSON-RPC error Tool Execution Error API failure, input validation error, business logic error A tool result with isError: true

Input validation errors sit in the second row. The specification says tool execution errors "contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters."

The script validate_input.py validates three sets of arguments against one schema.

Schema Validation With A Tool Execution Error
INPUT_SCHEMA = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "report_id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}$"}
    },
    "required": ["report_id"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
validator = Draft202012Validator(INPUT_SCHEMA)


def call_read_report(arguments):
    errors = [error.message for error in validator.iter_errors(arguments)]
    if errors:
        return {
            "resultType": "complete",
            "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Invalid arguments: " + "; ".join(errors)}],
            "isError": True,
        }
    return {
        "resultType": "complete",
        "content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"Report {arguments['report_id']} loaded."}],
        "isError": False,
    }
Output, 12 November 2026
{"report_id": "FR-2031"} -> {"resultType": "complete", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Report FR-2031 loaded."}], "isError": false}
{"report_id": "../../etc/passwd"} -> {"resultType": "complete", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Invalid arguments: '../../etc/passwd' does not match '^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}$'"}], "isError": true}
{"report_id": "FR-2031", "debug": true} -> {"resultType": "complete", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Invalid arguments: Additional properties are not allowed ('debug' was unexpected)"}], "isError": true}

The third call fails because the schema sets additionalProperties to false, so a field the tool never declared is refused.

docs.title: Keep Outputs Tight
docs.text:
A tool's output goes back into the model's context, and from there it can reach the user or another tool.

  • Schema - If a tool declares an outputSchema, servers MUST provide structured results that conform to it.
  • Size - OWASP's guide says to "Enforce size limits on all outputs from the tools or model."
  • Fields - It also says to "Only expose minimal, strictly necessary fields to the model".
  • Errors - "Do not return stack traces, tokens, filesystem paths, or tool internals in responses", in OWASP's words.

docs.title: Rate Limits
docs.text: Rate limiting is one of the four duties, and the specification leaves the numbers to you. OWASP's guide asks teams to "Impose quotas and rate limits on tool invocations and data fetches per session."

docs.title: State Handles Replaced Sessions
docs.text:
Revision 2026-07-28 removed protocol-level sessions. A server that needs state across calls, such as a shopping basket, now returns an explicit handle from a creation tool and accepts it back as an ordinary argument. MCP's security best practices describe the attack that follows, in which someone obtains or guesses a handle and uses it to reach another user's state.

Rule Source Wording Possession Proves Nothing MCP servers MUST NOT treat possession of a state handle as authentication. Verify Each Request MCP servers that implement authorization MUST verify all inbound requests. Make Handles Unguessable Servers SHOULD use secure, non-deterministic handles generated with secure random number generators. Bind Handles To The User Servers SHOULD bind handles server-side to the authenticated user, with the user ID derived from the verified token. State The Lifetime The retention policy should be stated in the creation tool's description. Report Expiry A call against an expired or unknown handle should return a tool execution error that says so.

The script state_handles.py stores each basket under the user ID and the handle together.

Handles Bound To The User
baskets = {}


def create_basket(user_id):
    handle = "bsk_" + secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
    baskets[(user_id, handle)] = []
    return handle


def add_item(user_id, handle, sku):
    basket = baskets.get((user_id, handle))
    if basket is None:
        return {"isError": True, "text": "Unknown or expired basket. Create a new one."}
    basket.append(sku)
    return {"isError": False, "text": f"Added {sku}. Basket holds {len(basket)} item(s)."}
Output, 12 November 2026
handle length: 26
owner: {'isError': False, 'text': 'Added SKU-1. Basket holds 1 item(s).'}
other user, same handle: {'isError': True, 'text': 'Unknown or expired basket. Create a new one.'}

A second user who presents the first user's handle gets the same answer as for a handle that never existed.

Reading Guidance Written Before July 2026

OWASP's guide dates from February 2026 and speaks of sessions. Its rule "Never rely on session IDs alone for authorization or authentication" matches what the specification now says about state handles. For servers on revision 2025-11-25 or earlier, the best practices page links to its earlier guidance on session hijacking.

Next: Logging After The July Change

docs.title: Logging After The July Change
docs.text:
After an incident, the first question is which tool ran, for which user and with which arguments. A server that can't answer has the gap OWASP lists as MCP08, Lack of Audit and Telemetry. Revision 2026-07-28 adds a second reason to review your logging, because it deprecated the protocol's own Logging feature.

Source - Protocol changes come from the specification's list of changes and its stdio transport page. Quoted logging advice comes from OWASP's server development guide.

docs.title: What Changed
docs.text: Item Revision 2026-07-28 logging/setLevel Removed. Log Level Set per request through io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel in _meta. Servers MUST NOT emit notifications/message for requests that did not include the field. Logging Feature Deprecated. It stays functional during the deprecation window, and new implementations should not add support for it. Suggested Migration Log to stderr on stdio, or use OpenTelemetry. Deprecation Window At least twelve months, under the specification's new feature lifecycle policy. Trace Context The revision documents OpenTelemetry trace context conventions for the _meta fields traceparent, tracestate and baggage.

docs.title: Where Logs Go Now
docs.text:
stdioStreamable HTTP

The server MAY write UTF-8 strings to stderr for any logging purpose. It MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, so a stray print statement there breaks the protocol stream.

The client MAY capture, forward or ignore the server's stderr output. A log line written only to stderr can therefore disappear, and audit records need a second destination that your team controls.

OpenTelemetry is the specification's suggested route. OWASP's guide adds the destination and says to "Feed MCP server audit logs into a centralized monitoring system (SIEM)."

docs.title: What To Record
docs.text:
• Tool Calls - "Log every action, including tool invocations (with parameters), resource access", in OWASP's words.
  • Scope Elevation - MCP's security best practices tell servers to "Log elevation events (scope requested, granted subset) with correlation IDs".
  • Failed Validation - OWASP's guide suggests real-time alerts "for suspicious patterns, such as a spike in failed validations".

docs.title: What To Keep Out
docs.text:
Tokens come first. The specification counts tokens "cached or logged on the server" among the ones attackers obtain. For everything else, OWASP's guide says to "Use field-level allowlists and redaction/hashing to prevent sensitive data from entering verbose logs."

The script audit_log.py writes one JSON line for each tool call and logs an argument in full only if the tool's allowlist names it.

An Audit Line With An Allowlist
LOGGED_FIELDS = {"send_report": {"report_id"}}


def audit(user_id, tool, arguments, is_error):
    allowed = LOGGED_FIELDS.get(tool, set())
    safe = {k: (v if k in allowed else "[REDACTED]") for k, v in arguments.items()}
    line = {
        "time": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime()),
        "event": "tools/call",
        "user": user_id,
        "tool": tool,
        "arguments": safe,
        "is_error": is_error,
    }
    print(json.dumps(line), file=sys.stderr)
Output On stderr, 12 November 2026
{"time": "2026-11-12T14:29:43Z", "event": "tools/call", "user": "user-17", "tool": "send_report", "arguments": {"report_id": "FR-2031", "api_key": "[REDACTED]"}, "is_error": false}

The call passed an api_key argument that the allowlist does not name, and the log line shows it redacted. Nothing was written to stdout.

OWASP's guide closes the loop on storage and says to "Store these logs securely and immutably for forensic analysis."

docs.title: Tokens And Scopes
docs.text:
A valid token is not always a token meant for your server. If your server accepts one that was issued for a different service, a token stolen there works here too. Scopes carry the second risk, because a token that holds every scope turns one leak into access to every tool.

Source - Requirements come from the authorization specification, its security considerations and MCP's security best practices. Quoted advice from OWASP comes from its server development guide.

docs.title: Check Who The Token Was Issued For
docs.text:
MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience. Invalid or expired tokens MUST receive an HTTP 401 response. OWASP's guide lists the checks for each request: "validate iss, aud, exp, and signatures on every request."

The script validate_token.py signs two test tokens with a throwaway key and validates both.

Audience And Issuer Validation
def validate(token, public_key):
    return jwt.decode(
        token,
        public_key,
        algorithms=["RS256"],
        audience=RESOURCE,
        issuer=ISSUER,
        options={"require": ["exp", "aud", "iss"]},
    )
Output, 12 November 2026
issued for this server: accepted
issued for another API: rejected, respond with HTTP 401 (Audience doesn't match)

docs.title: Never Pass A Client's Token Downstream
docs.text:
Many MCP servers call another API to do their work, and forwarding the client's token to that API looks like the short route. The specification calls it token passthrough and forbids it. An MCP server MUST NOT pass through the token it received from the MCP client. For upstream calls, the server acts as an OAuth client and uses a separate token issued by the upstream authorization server.

MCP's security best practices name four risks of passthrough.

  • Security Control Circumvention - Clients can use tokens directly with downstream APIs and bypass rate limiting, request validation or traffic monitoring.
  • Accountability And Audit Trail Issues - The MCP server cannot tell its clients apart, and downstream logs show requests under a different identity.
  • Trust Boundary Issues - If several services accept the same token, an attacker who compromises one of them can reach the others.
  • Future Compatibility Risk - A server that starts as a pure proxy may need security controls later, and separate token audiences make that change easier.

For delegation, OWASP's guide points to the OAuth token delegation flow in RFC 8693.

docs.title: Keep Scopes Small
docs.text:
The attack described in MCP's best practices starts with a server that lists every scope in scopes_supported and a client that requests them all. One stolen token then carries files:*, db:* and admin:*.

At First ContactAt A Privileged Call

Start with a minimal scope set that covers only low-risk discovery and read operations. The specification intends scopes_supported to be the minimal set needed for basic functionality. Servers SHOULD NOT include offline_access in it or in a WWW-Authenticate scope.

Answer with HTTP 403 and name the scopes the operation needs. Servers SHOULD include all scopes required for the current operation in a single challenge. The example below is the specification's own.

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope",
                         scope="files:write",
                         resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource",
                         error_description="File write permission required for this operation"
Status Code Usage In The Specification 401 Unauthorized Authorization required or token invalid 403 Forbidden Invalid scopes or insufficient permissions 400 Bad Request Malformed authorization request

docs.title: Scope Mistakes The Specification Names
docs.text:
• Publishing all possible scopes in scopes_supported
  • Using wildcard or omnibus scopes (*, all, full-access)
  • Bundling unrelated privileges to preempt future prompts
  • Returning the entire scope catalog in every challenge
  • Silent scope semantic changes without versioning
  • Treating claimed scopes in a token as sufficient without server-side authorization logic

A Scope Is A Claim, And Your Server Still Decides

The last mistake on that list pairs with a server duty in the tools specification, which says servers MUST implement proper access controls. A scope in a token tells your server what was granted. Your own authorization logic decides whether this user may run this tool on this record.

docs.title: Token Lifetime
docs.text:
Authorization servers SHOULD issue short-lived access tokens to reduce the impact of a leak. OWASP's guide is more specific and asks for "minimal lifetimes (minutes) and narrow scopes." The specification also counts tokens "cached or logged on the server" among the ones attackers obtain, which is one reason Logging After The July Change keeps tokens out of log lines.

Next: Inputs, Outputs And State Handles

docs.title: Deadbugz, August 2026
docs.text:
A security reviewer who installed productivity-suite and tried its two tools would have found nothing wrong. Both tools did their job. The server was built to wait until a client had made three tool calls, and only then did it start sending the agent instructions to hunt for credentials.

Source - Pillar Security disclosed the campaign on 12 August 2026 in a report by Ariel Fogel. The name comes from deadbug-mcp.py, a file the campaign used for delivery.

docs.title: How The Campaign Ran
docs.text:
1. 10 August 2026 - One public GitHub account opens 23 pull requests within 74 minutes. Pillar describes the targets as unrelated AI, MCP and developer-tool projects.
  2. The Requests - Seventeen add a remote MCP server to a project's configuration. Four point to a hidden local Python script, and two submit the server to directories or listings.
  3. First Contact - A client that connects finds two tools, format_text and summarize, each with a plain one-line description. They behave normally at first.
  4. The Counter - The server counts each client's tools/call requests in memory. Once the count reaches three, its tools/list and prompts/get responses change.
  5. The Switch - The new metadata directs the agent to seek SSH keys, AWS credentials, shell history and Kubernetes configuration, and to conceal the activity from the user.
  6. 12 August 2026 - Pillar publishes its disclosure and says it will update the report as verified information becomes available.

docs.title: What Is Established And What Isn't
docs.text:
Established By Pillar Not Established None of the 23 pull requests had been merged through GitHub's merge mechanism at the time of review. Nineteen were closed and four were open. Whether any organisation connected the server. Pillar reports no confirmed victim. The server's behaviour, which Pillar observed in its public source code and under test requests. How stolen data would leave a machine. The disclosure describes no exfiltration method. The source includes optional telemetry sent to a configured webhook address. Whether that telemetry carries stolen data, and who runs the campaign.

Do Not Test The Original

Pillar advises against running deadbug-mcp.py. Part 5 reproduces the delayed change with a harmless server built for this guide.

docs.title: Why A Review At Install Time Misses It
docs.text: A review at install time sees the definitions a server returns on its first response. In Deadbugz those definitions were clean, and the harmful text arrived only after normal use had begun. Pillar's message to the people who build MCP clients is that "Tool descriptions and schemas are a security boundary." It asks them to treat any change to an approved server's tool definitions as a security event that requires renewed approval.

docs.title: If You Find It In Your Environment
docs.text:
Pillar's disclosure lists the indicators to search for and gives five steps.

  • Block - Block the endpoint named in the disclosure.
  • Revert - Reject or revert any configuration change that adds the server.
  • Search - Look for Pillar's indicators across repositories and developer machines.
  • Preserve - Keep your MCP client logs.
  • Rotate - Rotate credentials under your incident-response policy.

OWASP's GenAI Security Project included the campaign in its exploit roundup for the third quarter of 2026.

Next: The WhatsApp Demonstration, April 2025

docs.title: The Fake Postmark Package, September 2025
docs.text:
Postmark publishes its MCP server on GitHub and, before September 2025, had never published one on npm. Someone else filled that gap. A package named postmark-mcp appeared on npm, built trust across 15 versions and then began copying the emails it sent to an outside address.

Source - Koi Security found the backdoor, and Postmark confirmed the incident in a statement on 25 September 2025. Koi's figures on these pages come from The Register's report of 29 September 2025.

15versions published before the backdoor, according to Postmark 1.0.16the version that added it, according to Postmark ~1,500downloads in a week, according to Koi Security 1customer known to have used it, Postmark told The Register

docs.title: What The Backdoor Did
docs.text:
Version 1.0.16 "added a backdoor" that "secretly BCC'd emails to an external server", in Postmark's words. The Register reports that the change was a single line of code. Its reporting adds that the developer appears to have copied the real server's code from GitHub and published it on npm under the look-alike name.

Postmark states that it had no involvement with the package, and that its own API and services remain secure and unaffected.

docs.title: Two Sets Of Numbers
docs.text: Koi Security counted about 1,500 downloads in a week. Idan Dardikman, Koi's co-founder and CTO, estimated that around 20 percent of those were in active use, which he put at about 300 organisations. Postmark told The Register that it knew of only one customer that used the package. No source has published a confirmed count of affected organisations.

docs.title: Code Changed, Descriptions Didn't Have To
docs.text: In the two earlier cases, a server fed instructions to the model through tool descriptions. The Postmark reports describe a change in the package's code, and none of them mentions a changed description. OWASP's MCP Security Cheat Sheet warns that pinning tool definitions by hash detects metadata changes only. A check of that kind would not catch a server whose code changes behind an unchanged definition.

docs.title: If You Installed It
docs.text:
Postmark gives three steps to anyone who used the fake package.

  • Remove - Remove the package from your systems right away.
  • Review - Check your email logs for suspicious activity.
  • Rotate - Consider rotating any credentials that were sent by email while the package was in use.

Postmark's official MCP server is at github.com/ActiveCampaign/postmark-mcp.

Next: The Cases Against OWASP's Beta List

docs.title: The Cases Against OWASP's Beta List
docs.text: Security teams often have to file a finding under a recognised category before anyone funds the fix. The OWASP MCP Top 10 supplies those categories for MCP. Treat it with some care, because OWASP's project page places the list at Phase 3, a beta release under pilot testing, and calls it a living document.

docs.title: The Ten Entries
docs.text: ID Entry MCP01 Token Mismanagement & Secret Exposure MCP02 Privilege Escalation via Scope Creep MCP03 Tool Poisoning MCP04 Software Supply Chain Attacks & Dependency Tampering MCP05 Command Injection & Execution MCP06 Prompt Injection via Contextual Payloads MCP07 Insufficient Authentication & Authorization MCP08 Lack of Audit and Telemetry MCP09 Shadow MCP Servers MCP10 Context Injection & Over-Sharing

docs.title: Where Each Case Fits
docs.text:
Case Closest Beta Entry OWASP's Wording For That Entry Deadbugz MCP03 Tool Poisoning "an adversary compromises the tools, plugins, or their outputs that an AI model depends on" WhatsApp, Experiment 1 MCP03 Tool Poisoning The same wording applies. WhatsApp, Experiment 2 MCP06 Prompt Injection via Contextual Payloads "in the MCP world the 'interpreter' is the model and the 'payload' is text" Fake Postmark Package MCP04 Software Supply Chain Attacks & Dependency Tampering "A compromised dependency can alter agent behavior or introduce execution-level backdoors."

The Pairings Are This Guide's Own

OWASP itself has not sorted these three cases into its MCP list. Each pairing in the table is this guide's own, based on the quoted wording of the entry.

docs.title: OWASP's Own Classification Of Deadbugz
docs.text:
OWASP's GenAI Security Project did classify Deadbugz in its exploit roundup for the third quarter of 2026, against two of its other lists. The roundup assigns the campaign no MCP Top 10 codes.

OWASP List Entries Assigned To Deadbugz Top 10 for Agentic Applications ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation Top 10 for LLM Applications LLM04:2026 Supply Chain, LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure

docs.title: Entries These Cases Don't Reach
docs.text: The three cases touch three of the ten entries. Token handling (MCP01), scope creep (MCP02), command injection (MCP05), authentication (MCP07), audit gaps (MCP08), shadow servers (MCP09) and over-sharing of context (MCP10) have no case on these pages. Parts 3 to 5 take them up from the builder's and the operator's side.

docs.title: The WhatsApp Demonstration, April 2025
docs.text:
Approval dialogs are the control most teams count on. Researchers at Invariant Labs showed in April 2025 how an agent can leak a user's WhatsApp messages while the user confirms every tool call.

Source - Luca Beurer-Kellner and Marc Fischer of Invariant Labs published the work on 7 April 2025. They built it as a demonstration to raise awareness of the risk. Invariant sells MCP security tools, and the post promotes them.

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
An agent in a client such as Cursor or Claude Desktop is connected to two servers. One is a trusted whatsapp-mcp server that can send, receive and check messages. The second belongs to the attacker.

Experiment 1: The Sleeper ServerExperiment 2: No Malicious Server

  1. On first launch, the attacker's server advertises one tool, get_fact_of_the_day, described as "Get a random fact of the day."
  2. The user approves the tool.
  3. On its second launch, the server swaps in a new description. The user isn't asked to approve again.
  4. The new description tells the agent to send WhatsApp messages to a proxy number, place the real recipient in the message body, attach the results of earlier list_chats calls and avoid notifying the user.
  5. The agent sends the user's chat data to the attacker through the trusted WhatsApp server.

The attacker needs only the target's WhatsApp number. A message that contains a prompt injection is sent to the target, and it takes effect once the agent calls list_chats and reads the message. Invariant reports that the injection was harder to get working and that it still succeeded.

docs.title: Why Approval Didn't Stop It
docs.text:
Invariant states that a user must always confirm a tool call before it runs, at least in Cursor and Claude Desktop. The confirmation showed a raw phone number as the recipient, which is hard to check by eye. The message appeared to read "Hi", and the stolen data sat far to the right, where the user would have to scroll to find it.

Sandboxing Would Not Have Helped

Invariant states that code isolation or sandboxing of the MCP server is not a relevant mitigation, because the attack relies on the agent's instruction-following. In the first experiment the data left through WhatsApp itself, sent by the trusted server at the agent's request.

Invariant's post gives no detailed list of fixes. Its one piece of general advice is to be cautious when connecting an agent to untrusted MCP servers.

Next: The Fake Postmark Package, September 2025

docs.title: The Three Roles: Host, Client, Server
docs.text:
A developer adds a few lines to a configuration file, and an AI assistant gains a new connection to company data. Behind those lines sit a host, a client and a server. Each holds a different share of the security work, and the MCP architecture assigns most of it to the host.

HOST The AI application. Holds the model and the full conversation. Client 1 Client 2 Client 3 stdio stdio Streamable HTTP Server Files LOCAL Server Database LOCAL Server External API REMOTE One host, one client for each server. Adapted from the MCP architecture page.

docs.title: Who Does What
docs.text:
Role What It Is Its Security Job In The Specification Host Your developers open the host every day. It's the AI application itself, a chat interface or an AI code editor for example, and it creates one client for every server they connect. Most of the load sits here. A host enforces security policies and consent requirements, controls each client's connection permissions and handles the user's authorization decisions. Client Three connected servers mean three clients. A client is a connector that lives inside the host and talks to exactly one server. Maintains the security boundaries between servers. Server The program behind the tools. It runs as a local process on the user's machine or as a remote service, and it exposes resources, prompts and tools to the client. Must respect security constraints. Where it offers tools, the specification says a server MUST validate all inputs, implement access controls, rate limit invocations and sanitize outputs.

MCP's design principles state that a server should not be able to read the whole conversation or see into other servers. The full conversation history stays with the host, and the host process enforces the boundaries.

There's a limit to that promise. The specification adds that MCP cannot enforce its security principles at the protocol level, so your protection depends on how the host your developers chose was built.

docs.title: Local And Remote Servers
docs.text:
A server runs either as a local process on the user's machine or as a remote service. Local servers usually communicate over stdio, the standard input and output streams of a process the client launches. Remote servers use Streamable HTTP, and the older HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated.

A Local Server Runs With The User's Access

OWASP's MCP Security Cheat Sheet notes that stdio avoids a listening endpoint. It does nothing to restrict the server process's access to files, the network or credentials. MCP's own security guidance asks clients to warn that a local server runs with the same privileges as the client.

docs.title: What A Server Can Offer
docs.text:
ToolsResourcesPrompts

Functions for the AI model to execute. A tool can query a database, call an API or perform a computation.

Context and data, for the user or the AI model to use.

Templated messages and workflows for users.

The specification singles out tools. It states that they represent arbitrary code execution and must be treated with appropriate caution.

Next: Why The Model Reads Tool Definitions

docs.title: Why The Model Reads Tool Definitions
docs.text:
Before a model can use a tool, the client asks the server for its tool list. The server answers with a definition for each tool, and the client passes those definitions to the model as context. Everything the model knows about a tool before the first call comes from text that the server's author wrote.

  1. The client sends a tools/list request to the server.
  2. The server returns its tool definitions.
  3. The client passes the definitions to the model as context.
  4. The model reads them and selects a tool for the user's request.
  5. The client sends a tools/call request, and the server runs the tool.

docs.title: Inside A Tool Definition
docs.text:
The example below comes from the MCP specification.

{
  "name": "get_weather", // (1)!
  "title": "Weather Information Provider",
  "description": "Get current weather information for a location", // (2)!
  "inputSchema": { // (3)!
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "location": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "City name or zip code" // (4)!
      }
    },
    "required": ["location"]
  }
}
  1. The tool's unique identifier within one server.
  2. Free text from the server's author. The model reads it to decide when and how to call the tool.
  3. A JSON Schema that defines the parameters the tool expects.
  4. Parameter descriptions are free text too, and the model reads them as well.

A definition can also carry annotations, optional properties that describe the tool's behaviour. The specification requires clients to treat annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.

docs.title: Text That Works As An Instruction
docs.text:
A description is written for the model, and a model is built to follow natural-language instructions. OWASP's MCP Security Cheat Sheet names the resulting risk tool poisoning, where malicious instructions hidden in tool descriptions, parameter schemas or return values manipulate the model's behaviour. OWASP advises treating the whole schema as a possible injection surface, parameter names and types included.

Research Demonstration, April 2025

Invariant Labs built a test server with one tool, get_fact_of_the_day. Its description told the agent to change the recipient of any WhatsApp message sent through a second, trusted server. In the researchers' demonstration, the agent sent the user's WhatsApp chat data to a number they controlled. Nobody was attacked, and the work was a proof of concept. Part 2 walks through it step by step.

docs.title: One Server Can Steer Another's Tools
docs.text: The model sees tool descriptions from every connected server in the same context, as OWASP's cheat sheet points out. A description from one server can therefore change how the agent uses a tool from another, a risk OWASP lists as tool shadowing. In the Invariant Labs test, the untrusted server never touched WhatsApp itself.

docs.title: Definitions Can Change
docs.text:
A tool list isn't fixed. The specification allows the set of tools to change over time, and a server that declares listChanged should notify clients that subscribed to updates. OWASP uses the term rug pull for the harmful case, where a server changes its tool definitions after the user's initial approval.

The Practical Consequence

Reviewing a server's tools once tells you what they said on that day. Part 5 covers how to record approved definitions and detect a change.

Next: What The Protocol Leaves To You

docs.title: What The Protocol Leaves To You
docs.text: MCP's maintainers wrote a plain admission into the specification. The protocol, they state, cannot enforce its security principles at the protocol level. They sort every requirement with fixed keywords, and the gap between MUST, SHOULD and OPTIONAL marks where your own work begins.

docs.title: Reading The Keywords
docs.text:
The keywords follow RFC 2119 and carry their formal meaning only in capitals.

MUSTSHOULDOPTIONAL

An absolute requirement. An implementation that skips it does not conform to the specification.

A recommendation. RFC 2119 accepts that valid reasons may exist to ignore it in particular circumstances.

A free choice. One vendor may include the item and another may leave it out.

docs.title: Where The Specification Stops
docs.text:
Area What The Specification States Left To Your Team Authorization OPTIONAL for MCP implementations. HTTP-based transports SHOULD follow the authorization specification when they support it. Requiring it on every remote server that exposes non-public tools or data. Human Approval There SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations. Choosing which actions need confirmation, and checking that your host asks for it. Tool Annotations Clients MUST consider them untrusted unless they come from trusted servers. Deciding which servers your organisation trusts, and on what evidence. Tool Inputs And Outputs Servers MUST validate all tool inputs, implement access controls, rate limit invocations and sanitize outputs. Confirming that a server you didn't write does so. Audit Logs Clients SHOULD log tool usage for audit purposes. Verifying that your host keeps those logs and that someone reviews them. Local Server Setup A client with one-click setup MUST show the exact command without truncation and require explicit approval. Reading the command before anyone approves it.

A Requirement Binds Only Those Who Follow It

A MUST tells an honest developer what to build. A hostile server's author has no reason to comply, so each requirement placed on servers still needs a check from your side.

docs.title: A Specification That Keeps Moving
docs.text:
MCP's rules change between revisions. Revision 2026-07-28 removed protocol-level sessions and the initialize handshake, and every request now carries its own protocol version and client capabilities. Security advice built around session IDs applies to revision 2025-11-25 and earlier.

The same revision deprecated Dynamic Client Registration in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents, and it deprecated the protocol's Logging feature. Before you apply any published guidance, check which revision your host and servers implement.
